fig15_1: Three horizontal rows of dots over the interval from minus one to one, comparing quadrature node placements for thirty-two points. The Newton-Cotes row shows evenly spaced dots; the Gauss-Legendre and Clenshaw-Curtis rows both crowd their dots tightly toward the two endpoints and thin them out in the middle, visually conveying that the latter two share the same endpoint-clustered distribution that suppresses the Runge phenomenon.
fig15_2: Semilog plot of monomial quadrature error versus monomial degree k from zero to sixty-four for three rules using thirty-three points. The coral Newton-Cotes and teal Clenshaw-Curtis curves hug the machine-precision floor near ten to the power minus sixteen up to degree thirty-two, then climb steeply once k exceeds n. The navy Gauss-Legendre curve stays flat at the floor across the entire range, since its degree of precision sixty-five exceeds every test degree. Odd-degree points sit on the floor by symmetry.
fig15_3: Semilog plot of absolute quadrature error against the number of points n for the Runge function one over one plus twenty-five x squared. The red Newton-Cotes curve climbs steeply upward, diverging roughly like two to the power n, while the navy Gauss-Legendre and teal Clenshaw-Curtis curves plunge rapidly toward machine precision. The contrast shows that equal degree of precision does not guarantee accuracy.
tbl15_1: Table reporting Newton-Cotes errors with thirty points for monomials x to the k and Chebyshev polynomials T sub k across degrees twenty-six to thirty-eight, showing both are exactly zero below the exactness degree but above it the monomial errors stay tiny (around ten to the power minus four to minus seven) while the Chebyshev errors explode into the hundreds and tens of thousands, exposing the rule's hidden ill-conditioning.
fig15_4: Semilog convergence plot of the error in integrating e to the power x on minus one to one against the number of points, validating from-scratch Gauss-Legendre (Golub-Welsch) and Clenshaw-Curtis (FFT) implementations. Both error curves descend steadily and level off at machine precision near ten to the power minus sixteen, confirming the rules were built correctly.
fig15_5: Grid of six semilog convergence panels, one per benchmark function of decreasing smoothness (a degree-twenty polynomial, two entire functions, an analytic function with nearby poles, a C-infinity function, and a C-two function), each plotting quadrature error against n from one to thirty-two for Gauss (filled circles) and Clenshaw-Curtis (open circles). For the polynomial Gauss reaches the floor at half the points, but for the analytic and less smooth functions the two marker sets fall almost on top of each other, showing the two methods are essentially indistinguishable in practice.
fig15_6: Two semilog panels for n equals thirty. Left: Clenshaw-Curtis error for the Chebyshev polynomial T sub k versus even k, sitting at zero up to k equals twenty-eight, then staying small (order n to the power minus two) across a shaded band from thirty to sixty before rising to order one beyond. Right: for the function absolute value of x cubed, the products of Chebyshev coefficient magnitude times quadrature error versus k, showing the shaded-band terms do not dominate the total error, which explains why Clenshaw-Curtis stays accurate.
fig15_7: Four-panel grid for n equals sixteen. Panels (a), (b), (c) are complex-plane contour maps of the approximation error between the exact kernel phi and the rational approximant r sub n for Newton-Cotes, Gauss-Legendre, and Clenshaw-Curtis, with the innermost contour at one and outer contours at ten to the power minus one, minus two, and so on; the Newton-Cotes contours are pinched tightly against the real interval while the Gauss and Clenshaw-Curtis contours look virtually identical. Panel (d) is a semilog convergence plot on the Runge-like integral one over one plus sixteen x squared, where Newton-Cotes diverges upward while Gauss and Clenshaw-Curtis descend geometrically together to machine precision by about a hundred points.
fig15_8: Two panels on the Gauss-Hermite paradox. Left: scatter of the hundred quadrature weights for n equals one hundred plotted on a log scale against node position, with a horizontal dashed line at machine precision ten to the power minus sixteen; roughly half the weights fall below the line, marking them as computationally useless. Right: the fraction of weights below machine precision rising with n and tending toward one hundred percent as n grows, showing the waste worsens with order.
fig15_9: Semilog plot of quadrature error against the number of points for the integral of e to the power minus x squared times cosine of x cubed over the whole real line. The navy Gauss-Hermite curve descends slowly along a parabolic root-exponential path, while the coral truncated trapezoidal rule on minus six to six drops far more steeply and reaches machine precision around eighty points, dramatically beating the formally optimal Hermite rule.
fig15_10: Two semilog panels verifying asymptotic convergence rates by rescaling the horizontal axis. Left: Gauss-Hermite error plotted against the square root of n falls along a straight line, confirming a root-exponential rate of order e to the power minus C times square root of n. Right: truncated Gauss-Legendre error plotted against n to the two-thirds power also forms a straight line, confirming the steeper rate e to the power minus C times n to the two-thirds; dashed least-squares fit lines mark the slopes used to extract the decay constants.
